summary:
FieldShift is an agricultural environmental intelligence platform designed to help farmers in Sindh, Pakistan, explore environmental conditions and compare potential crop rotation strategies using NASA Earth observation data.

The platform integrates three NASA datasets: SMAP for root-zone soil moisture, GPM IMERG for precipitation, and MODIS NDVI for vegetation greenness. These observations are processed using Google Earth Engine and combined with administrative boundaries from the Humanitarian Data Exchange (HDX) COD-AB dataset to provide interactive environmental insights across 29 districts of Sindh.

Through an interactive map and environmental dashboard, users can explore district-level indicators, compare environmental patterns, and examine three candidate crop rotations: Rice–Wheat, Cotton–Wheat, and Mungbean–Wheat. Each rotation includes indicative crop water requirements, growing seasons, potential soil contributions, benefits, and constraints.

FieldShift aims to make complex satellite information more accessible and connect environmental awareness with agricultural planning. Its initial implementation uses January 2024 satellite observations and provides a foundation for future multi-season monitoring, regularly updated data, and locally validated agricultural decision support.
details:
The Problem We Want to Address

Farmers make important decisions about what to grow, when to grow it, and how to manage their available resources. These decisions are closely connected to environmental conditions such as soil moisture, rainfall, and vegetation health. However, satellite-derived environmental information is not always easy for farmers to access, interpret, or connect with agricultural planning.

FieldShift aims to bridge this gap by transforming NASA Earth observation data into an accessible, district-level agricultural intelligence platform for farmers in Sindh, Pakistan.

How FieldShift Works

FieldShift brings together three NASA satellite datasets to help users explore environmental conditions across 29 districts of Sindh:

  • NASA SMAP (Soil Moisture Active Passive): Provides root-zone soil moisture observations that help users explore variations in soil moisture conditions.
  • NASA GPM IMERG (Global Precipitation Measurement): Provides precipitation observations to explore rainfall patterns.
  • NASA MODIS MOD13Q1: Provides Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), an indicator of vegetation greenness.

We processed these datasets using Google Earth Engine and integrated the resulting district-level indicators into a unified dataset.

To establish the geographic framework, we obtained Pakistan's administrative boundaries from the Humanitarian Data Exchange (HDX) Common Operational Datasets for Administrative Boundaries (COD-AB), using the pak_admin_boundaries.shp.zip dataset. We extracted Sindh's 29 districts and integrated their boundaries into the platform.

Through an interactive map, users can select a district, explore individual NASA data layers, visualize environmental patterns, and compare district-level observations through charts and indicators.

Exploring Crop Rotation Strategies

Beyond environmental visualization, FieldShift introduces a crop rotation comparison feature designed around agricultural planning considerations.

The platform presents three candidate crop sequences:

  1. Rice → Wheat
  2. Cotton → Wheat
  3. Mungbean → Wheat

For each sequence, users can explore crop growing seasons, indicative water requirements, crop duration, potential soil contributions, benefits, risks, and constraints.

The inclusion of mungbean introduces an important soil-health consideration: legumes can contribute to biological nitrogen fixation under suitable conditions.

Rather than presenting one crop rotation as universally suitable, FieldShift allows users to examine different options and understand their potential trade-offs alongside environmental observations.

Who Benefits and Why It Matters

Our primary intended users are farmers in Sindh, particularly those interested in understanding local environmental conditions and exploring alternatives to familiar crop sequences.

FieldShift aims to make satellite-derived information easier to understand and more relevant to agricultural planning discussions. It can also serve agricultural extension workers, researchers, and planners who need an accessible way to explore district-level environmental patterns.

By bringing soil moisture, precipitation, vegetation indicators, and crop rotation information into one platform, FieldShift creates a starting point for more informed conversations about agricultural adaptation and resource management.

Technology and Development

FieldShift was developed using:

  • NASA Earth observation datasets: SMAP SPL4SMGP V008, GPM IMERG V07, and MODIS MOD13Q1 V061.
  • Google Earth Engine: Satellite data processing and district-level extraction.
  • Python and Pandas: Data cleaning, integration, and processing.
  • FastAPI: Backend services and environmental data APIs.
  • React and Vite: Interactive frontend application.
  • Leaflet and React-Leaflet: Geographic visualization and interactive district mapping.
  • GeoJSON: Sindh administrative boundary representation.
  • HTML and CSS: Interface design and styling.
  • Humanitarian Data Exchange (HDX): Pakistan administrative boundary source.

What Makes FieldShift Different

FieldShift connects multiple dimensions of agricultural environmental information instead of presenting satellite observations as isolated datasets. It combines NASA-derived soil moisture, precipitation, and vegetation indicators with an interactive district map and an exploratory crop rotation comparison feature.

Its district-focused approach makes the information geographically understandable, while its crop rotation component connects environmental awareness with practical agricultural questions.

Design Considerations and Future Potential

FieldShift's initial implementation demonstrates district-level analysis using January 2024 satellite observations across Sindh. The platform is designed as a foundation that can be expanded with additional observation periods, regularly updated satellite data, more environmental indicators, and locally validated crop profiles.

We recognize that district averages cannot describe every individual farm, and that crop decisions also depend on factors such as soil salinity, soil texture, irrigation availability, planting calendars, and local agronomic knowledge. The current crop rotations are exploratory candidates, not automated farm-level prescriptions or yield predictions.

Our longer-term vision is to make FieldShift a more comprehensive agricultural decision-support resource that helps farmers and agricultural stakeholders connect Earth observation data with local knowledge.

FieldShift's goal is simple: make the power of NASA Earth observation data more accessible to the people whose livelihoods depend on the land.
